key_insight: Error-Conditioned Neural Solvers make neural PDE surrogates self-correct by learning how to react to their own mistakes, rather than relying only on a one-shot prediction. This enables faster and more stable refinement toward physically valid solutions without the full cost of classical optimization.
problem_solved: The paper addresses the weakness of standard neural surrogate solvers: they can be fast, but they often violate PDE constraints, struggle to fix their own errors, and perform poorly outside the training distribution. Existing hybrid correction methods improve physical consistency, but usually depend on expensive and unstable gradient-based optimization.
method: Train a neural solver to condition its update on the current error or residual, so it learns a correction rule instead of only a direct parameter-to-solution map.
Use the model’s own predicted violation signals to iteratively refine solutions toward PDE consistency.
Reduce dependence on classical optimizers like gradient descent or Gauss--Newton, aiming for faster and more robust correction steps.
impact: For ML practitioners working on scientific computing, this offers a practical path to combine speed and physical correctness. It can make neural PDE solvers more reliable for out-of-distribution cases and reduce inference-time compute compared with traditional iterative correction methods.
